summary:
Şanlıurfa is a province of Turkey and stands under the Turkish national framework. The source inventory assembled for this province contains no trans-specific provincial material: no statute, enforcement action, facility, or recorded incident for Şanlıurfa itself. A trans visitor to the province should therefore expect the national regime as documented below.

Human Rights Watch reported on 29 October 2025 on a leaked omnibus draft, the 11th Judicial Package, that would amend the Turkish penal code to criminalise conduct deemed "contrary to biological sex and general morality", carrying up to three years in prison, and would criminalise participation in same-sex engagement or marriage ceremonies with up to four years. As of that reporting the draft had not been enacted.

The same draft would raise the minimum age for gender-affirming care, surgery included, from 18 to 25, conditioned on mandatory permanent infertility and repeated evaluations at government-approved hospitals. Healthcare professionals performing such interventions would face fines and up to seven years in prison, and patients up to three years, with pretrial detention possible. Fifteen LGBT groups and the Turkish Medical Association opposed the draft. Human Rights Watch warned that the measure would push treatment underground and leave LGBT people in constant fear of arrest.

Kaos GL's 2025 review, "The Year of the Family: A Major Siege Against LGBTI+ People", finds that hostility toward LGBTI+ people became explicit state policy: "Year of the Family" instructions were issued to public institutions, an LGBTI+ rights organisation was closed for the first time in years, expression and artistic freedom were restricted, and events were cancelled or banned.

The same monitoring records six right-to-life violations in 2025, including three hate-motivated killings, with transgender people the most affected group; 89 torture and ill-treatment violations, against 51 the previous year; 313 liberty violations, roughly two and a half times the previous year's figure, including 299 detention decisions; private-life violations rising from 16 to 67, among them obstruction of trans people's hormone therapy; and 61 travel bans.

The national framework also governs the mechanics a visitor meets on the ground. Police conduct street-level identity checks on trans people and require foreigners to produce original identity documents at such encounters, so any stoppage risks a comparison between passport gender marker and presentation. Trans prisoners are placed according to registered sex rather than gender identity, and the Health Ministry's 2025 reporting rules restrict how gender-related care is recorded in official medical documents.
tangentialFactors:
The year-on-year movement in the monitoring figures indicates a deteriorating position rather than a stable one: liberty violations rose to roughly two and a half times the prior year, torture and ill-treatment violations rose from 51 to 89, and private-life violations rose from 16 to 67.

The criminalising measures described by Human Rights Watch are a leaked draft rather than enacted law, and the reporting is explicit that it had not been passed at the time of publication. Its practical effect rests on the trajectory it signals, alongside the pattern already documented in enforcement.

Neither national source offers a provincial breakdown, so the figures cited here describe Turkey as a whole and cannot be attributed to Şanlıurfa in particular. Şanlıurfa's position relative to larger metropolitan centres such as Istanbul, where street-level checks of trans women have been recorded, is not addressed by the inventory.

Two institutional actors are on record opposing the draft: fifteen LGBT organisations and the Turkish Medical Association, the professional body representing the clinicians the draft would penalise.
localsOnly:
Residents, as distinct from visitors, are the direct subjects of the restrictions in the draft package: the raised age threshold and infertility condition would govern their access to gender-affirming care, and patients themselves would face up to three years' imprisonment for undergoing such interventions.

Kaos GL records obstruction of trans people's hormone therapy among the private-life violations of 2025, so continuity of existing treatment is exposed even before any new statute takes effect.

The 61 travel bans documented in the monitoring affect residents' ability to leave the country, a restriction that does not apply to foreign visitors.

Residents are the population subject to the 299 detention decisions recorded in 2025 and to the placement of trans prisoners by registered sex, with a trans man reported held in a women's prison.

Restrictions on expression, artistic freedom and event permits recorded by Kaos GL constrain resident organizing and public visibility directly.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the 11th Judicial Package has since been enacted is unresolved: the inventory contains only the 29 October 2025 report of a leaked draft that had not been passed at that date, and no later source confirming its status.

No Şanlıurfa-specific enforcement data is sourced. Whether identity checks, detentions or event bans have occurred in the province, and how local authorities apply national policy, are not addressed by any source in the inventory.

The circumstances of the LGBTI+ rights organisation's closure recorded by Kaos GL are unresolved: the inventory does not identify the organisation, the legal instrument used, or whether the closure was judicial or administrative.

Whether the draft's proposed care-age threshold has altered current clinical practice in Turkey is not sourced; the inventory records the proposed change and opposition to it, not its implementation.
